question: What is the primary goal of risk management in a healthcare setting?

options.A: Preventing harm to patients and staff
options.B: Reducing the length of patient hospital stays
options.C: Punishing staff who make clinical errors

explanation: The core purpose of healthcare risk management is to systematically identify and reduce hazards to keep patients, staff, and visitors safe from harm. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h1)

question: How should a healthcare facility properly treat a near miss event?

options.A: As proof of severe negligence requiring immediate suspension
options.B: As an isolated mistake caused entirely by carelessness
options.C: As a valuable learning opportunity to fix system flaws
options.D: As a minor occurrence that requires no formal documentation

explanation: Near misses highlight vulnerabilities in safety processes without causing actual injury, allowing organizations to fix them proactively before a real accident happens. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which element is essential for successful risk management in any hospital?

options.A: Active involvement and participation from frontline staff
options.B: Relying entirely on verbal communication without written logs
options.C: Outsourcing all safety protocols to external consultants
options.D: Strictly punishing every minor clinical mistake

explanation: Frontline workers like nurses spot daily hazards first, making their active engagement vital for spotting and resolving risks. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h2)

question: A hospital ward notices a rising trend in patient falls over three months. What risk management element is best used to address this?

options.A: Systematic data tracking and trend analysis
options.B: Stopping all physical therapy activities permanently
options.C: Immediate dismissal of the shift in-charge
options.D: Ignoring the data until a major injury occurs

explanation: Reviewing collected incident data helps identify patterns so targeted safety interventions can be implemented. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h2)

question: What is the very first step in managing clinical risks in a ward?

options.A: Writing a lengthy research paper on safety
options.C: Identifying potential hazards before harm occurs
options.D: Punishing the nurse responsible for an error

explanation: Risk management starts with recognizing and spotting hazards in the clinical environment before they turn into actual patient injuries. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h3)

question: Why do hospitals prioritize high-frequency, high-severity risks during analysis?

options.A: They require no financial budget to correct
options.B: They are the easiest administrative issues to fix quickly
options.C: They only affect hospital equipment and never human lives
options.D: They cause the most frequent and severe harm to patients

explanation: Risks that happen often and cause major injury pose the greatest threat to patient safety and demand immediate action. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is the main focus of a proactive risk mitigation strategy?

options.A: Punishing staff members after an adverse drug reaction
options.B: Preventing errors before they happen to patients
options.C: Writing incident reports days after a clinical mistake
options.D: Investigating accidents after the patient has been discharged

explanation: Proactive strategies anticipate potential failures and put safeguards in place to stop them before an incident occurs. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h4)

question: Which nursing action is an example of a reactive risk mitigation approach?

options.A: Double-checking high-alert medications with a colleague
options.B: Conducting a review meeting after a patient fall occurs
options.C: Teaching hand hygiene techniques to incoming students
options.D: Checking the crash cart daily before the morning shift

explanation: Reactive strategies take place after an adverse event has already happened to figure out what went wrong and prevent repetition. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting a Root Cause Analysis after an adverse event?

options.A: Finding a specific nurse to blame for the mistake
options.B: Complying with paperwork without making any changes
options.C: Uncovering underlying system flaws that allowed the error
options.D: Justifying an increase in hospital treatment fees

explanation: Root Cause Analysis looks beyond surface human error to find systemic issues that need fixing to prevent future incidents. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why do healthcare workers sometimes fail to submit incident reports in clinical practice?

options.A: Incidents never actually happen in busy hospital wards
options.B: Lack of interest in improving patient care quality
options.C: Fear of punishment or disciplinary action from management
options.D: Hospital policies that forbid writing down mistakes

explanation: A punitive culture creates fear, causing staff to hide mistakes rather than report them for institutional learning. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why are bedside nurses considered critical defenders against clinical errors?

options.A: They hold the final financial authority in the hospital
options.B: They only work during low-risk morning shifts
options.C: They write all the hospital administrative policies
options.D: They provide direct, continuous care on the front line

explanation: Because nurses spend the most time directly with patients, they are uniquely positioned to catch and stop potential safety hazards. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h6)

question: A nurse notices that two patients have very similar names in adjacent beds. What immediate safety action should be taken?

options.A: Use two unique patient identifiers before any medication administration
options.B: Ignore the similarity since staff know the ward well
options.C: Wait until a medication error happens to report the name similarity
options.D: Ask the patients to swap beds without informing the doctor

explanation: Using at least two patient identifiers prevents mix-ups between patients with similar names during treatments and procedures. [learn more](GST319_U4_T6#GST319_U4_T6_h6)
